claims.text: Spin-polarized density functional theory can predict the presence of ferromagnetic ground states in materials.
Spin-polarized DFT explicitly accounts for exchange splitting of electronic states.
Spin-polarized DFT permits comparison of the energy of a magnetic state with that of a non-magnetic state.
Modern exchange-correlation functionals can capture magnetic interactions.
Magnetic ordering can develop at low temperature or near equilibrium.
Accurate treatment of localized magnetic moments depends on the exchange-correlation functional.
Local electronic-orbital interactions on magnetic atoms or ions mediate the magnetic behavior.
Introducing spin polarization into the computational model produces exchange splitting in the electronic structure.
Exchange splitting can lower the total energy when ferromagnetic ordering is favorable.
Lowering the total energy through exchange splitting can stabilize a ferromagnetic ground state.
For a ferromagnetic ground state, DFT will give the ferromagnetic configuration a lower total energy than non-magnetic and antiferromagnetic configurations.
A predicted ferromagnetic state will have non-zero local magnetic moments on atomic sites.
Non-spin-polarized DFT or methods omitting magnetic exchange interactions would fail to predict a stabilized ferromagnetic ground state.
The accuracy of spin-polarized DFT predictions of magnetism is limited by the choice of exchange-correlation functional.
Spin-polarized DFT may be less reliable for strongly correlated or itinerant-electron systems.
Calculated magnetic energy differences and moment sizes may vary with computational parameters.
Quantitative magnetic predictions remain somewhat uncertain without experimental validation.
